task: R2 has an installed default route to the ISP and a working OSPF relationship with R1. Advertise a default into OSPF only while R2 retains that route; do not force advertisement or change the default metric.

teaching.hint: The branch needs an advertised default, but withdrawal must follow route availability.
teaching.takeaway: Without always, origination depends on an eligible installed default. That route’s presence still does not prove the upstream application is healthy; test the service separately.

task: R1’s GUEST-IN ACL is inbound on the guest gateway. Sequence 70 permits source 10.10.20.0/24, but a new client has no lease: its DHCP Discover is UDP 0.0.0.0:68 to 255.255.255.255:67. Add sequence 10 permitting client-to-server DHCP with any source and destination address.
answer: 10 permit udp any eq 68 any eq 67

teaching.hint: A new client cannot match a permit that assumes it already owns a guest-subnet address.
teaching.takeaway: The initial Discover has source 0.0.0.0, so the guest-subnet permit misses it. The earlier UDP rule admits the stated allocation traffic; other guest traffic still reaches the later restrictions.

task: After renumbering, guest 10.20.20.50 has a working gateway and route. Its fresh external HTTP request passes GUEST-IN but creates no PAT entry; staff traffic still works. Investigation found the old guest permit in NAT-LANS, and that obsolete entry has been removed. Add the new guest /24 permit without replacing the staff entry.

teaching.hint: Compare the actual inside source with the translation selector, not with the interface filter.
teaching.takeaway: A NAT selector miss leaves eligible routing traffic untranslated; it is not itself an ACL drop. The ISP has no private return route here, so verify a new guest translation and retest staff service after the correction.
